requirements: Reproduce the queueing-theoretic framework, empirical batch-processing-time modeling, throughput-optimality analysis, and experimental demonstrations from 'Throughput-Optimal Scheduling Algorithms for LLM Inference and AI Agents'.

sub_tasks.requirements: Hardware, software, model, and dataset dependencies required to run the LLM serving systems (FasterTransformer, vLLM, Orca, Sarathi-Serve, SGLang) and reproduce the experiments are available and configured.
GPU hardware environment matching the paper's experimental setup is provisioned.
Code has been implemented to detect/require NVIDIA A100 (80GB) GPU(s) matching the paper's setup for CodeLlama-34B and Llama-3-70B experiments (Figure 1, Figure 3, Figure 4, Figure 9).
The multi-GPU environment provides NVLink interconnect for tensor-parallel Llama-3-70B execution on two A100 80GB GPUs as specified in Section 2.1.
Code has been implemented to support running experiments with tensor-parallel sizes TP=1, TP=2, and TP=4 as used in Figure 4's piecewise-linear fits for CodeLlama-34B and Llama-70B.
Software dependencies (CUDA, PyTorch, and the specific LLM serving frameworks used in experiments) are installed and importable.
Code has been implemented to install and expose a CUDA-enabled PyTorch environment compatible with A100 GPUs (CUDA runtime accessible from Python; torch.cuda.is_available() returns True).
FasterTransformer (NVIDIA) is installed/built and can be launched to serve CodeLlama-34B for the Figure 1 stability experiment.
A version of vLLM that supports disabling chunked-prefill (vanilla vLLM behavior: prefill-prioritized without mixed batching) is installed and configurable, per Section 3.
Sarathi-Serve (or an equivalent chunked-prefill token-budget scheduler) is installed and exposes a configurable token budget parameter (values 128, 512, 1024) as used in Figures 1 and 9.
SGLang is installed and can serve models under high load with configurable token budgets (128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048) as used in the Figure 3 batch-processing-time measurements.
Either the Orca serving system or a documented functionally-equivalent prefill-prioritized-with-mixed-batching scheduler implementation is available for comparison as described in Section 3.
Infrastructure for driving each serving system with the paper's request workloads (arrival processes, prefill/decode lengths) is in place.

Code has been implemented for a request-generating client that issues requests to a running LLM serving endpoint at a configurable QPS (e.g., 14.3 QPS for Figure 1) with configurable prefill/decode token lengths.
Code has been implemented to generate Poisson request arrivals with configurable per-type rates for the Rybko-Stolyar-type two-agent LLM network simulation (Section 4.3).
Code has been implemented to drive experiments using the ShareGPT dataset for varied prefill/decode compositions in Figure 3 measurements.
Instrumentation to measure the quantities plotted in Figures 1, 3, 4, and 9 is available.
Code has been implemented to record the number of requests-in-system over wall-clock time for each serving system to reproduce Figure 1's time series.
Code has been implemented to log per-iteration batch processing time and per-iteration token load, enabling reproduction of the Figure 3 CoV analysis and Figure 4 piecewise-linear fit data.
Code has been implemented to record per-request end-to-end latency and TTFT (time-to-first-token) for CCDF plots in Figure 9.
Configuration and reproducibility scaffolding for scheduler settings and experiment runs is available.
Code has been implemented to expose the token budget parameter b (values 128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048) as a runtime-configurable option to each supported scheduler.
Code has been implemented to seed all random components (arrival process, token length sampling, dataset shuffles) so that experiments are deterministically reproducible.
Runnable entry-point scripts (or equivalent) are provided that launch each of the Figure 1, Figure 3, Figure 4, and Figure 9 experiments end-to-end from raw config to logged results.

The LLM models (CodeLlama-34B, Llama-3-70B, and 1B/8B variants) and datasets (ShareGPT, production conversation traces) used across empirical measurements are available and configured with the correct tensor-parallel setups.
The LLM model artifacts required by all experiments (CodeLlama-34B, Llama-3-70B, and the 1B/8B variants used in Figure 3) are acquired and loadable by the serving engines.

Code has been implemented to acquire the CodeLlama-34B model weights from a standard model hub (e.g., Hugging Face) with correct tokenizer and configuration files for use in Figure 1, Figure 8, and Figure 9 experiments.

Code has been implemented to acquire the Llama-3-70B (or equivalent Llama-70B) model weights with tokenizer/config, as needed to fit the piecewise-linear batch processing time curves in Figure 4 (right).

Code has been implemented to acquire the 1B and 8B Llama-family model variants (weights, tokenizer, config) needed to reproduce the batch-processing-time coefficient-of-variation curves shown for the 1B and 8B lines in Figure 3.

Code has been implemented to verify each acquired model can be loaded end-to-end (weights + tokenizer) and run a smoke-test forward pass at a small batch, so downstream serving-engine benchmarks are guaranteed a functioning model.
Tensor-parallel deployment configurations are set up so each model runs at the TP degree used in the paper's experiments on A100 GPUs.
Code has been implemented to launch CodeLlama-34B with TP=1, TP=2, and TP=4 tensor-parallel configurations, matching the three TP curves reported for CodeLlama-34B in Figure 4 (left).

Code has been implemented to launch Llama-3-70B with TP=2 and TP=4 tensor-parallel configurations, matching the two TP curves reported for Llama-70B in Figure 4 (right) (including the paper's stated TP=2 setup with two A100 80GB GPUs and NVLink).
The Figure 1 stability experiment is configured to use CodeLlama-34B on a single A100 GPU (single-engine setup), matching the paper's stated hardware/model configuration for that experiment.

Code has been implemented to programmatically verify at launch that the requested tensor-parallel size matches the number of GPUs actually allocated to the engine process, preventing silent TP misconfiguration.
The datasets used to drive request arrivals (ShareGPT for Figure 3 profiling and production conversation traces for Figure 9) are acquired and preprocessed into a form the serving engines can replay.

Code has been implemented to download the ShareGPT multi-turn conversation dataset (per the ShareGPT Contributors 2024 reference) and store it locally for use as the prompt source in Figure 3 batch-processing-time measurements.

Code has been implemented to parse ShareGPT records into (prefill_tokens, decode_tokens) pairs using each target model's tokenizer, producing request-length distributions that can be sampled to build batches of varying prefill/decode composition as required by Figure 3.

Code has been implemented to load the production conversation trace (or a documented publicly available substitute with the same arrival-rate and length statistics) and to scale its arrival rate to the high-load setting used in Figure 9 for CodeLlama-34B.

Code has been implemented to construct the homogeneous synthetic workload used in Figure 1: requests with average 129 prefill tokens and 112 decode tokens arriving at 14.3 queries per second (Poisson arrivals), so the same workload can be replayed against FasterTransformer, vanilla vLLM, and Sarathi-Serve.

Code has been implemented to emit a unified request-trace format (arrival_time, prompt_token_ids, target_decode_length) consumable by all serving engines under evaluation, so identical workloads drive every scheduler comparison.
Empirical dataset-level statistics claimed by the paper are validated against the prepared workloads.
The mean prefill length of the Figure 1 homogeneous workload, measured over the generated trace, equals 129 tokens (within a small tolerance) using the CodeLlama-34B tokenizer.
The mean decode length of the Figure 1 homogeneous workload, measured over the generated trace, equals 112 tokens (within a small tolerance).
The empirical arrival rate of the replayed Figure 1 trace equals 14.3 queries per second (within a small tolerance) over the measurement window.

The discrete-time stochastic processing model of the LLM engine (arrivals, iteration-level batch serving, feasibility constraints, DTMC state, system dynamics) from Section 2 is implemented faithfully.
The arrival process module correctly generates ordered requests with iid inter-arrival counts and iid (prefill-tokens, decode-tokens, feature) triples as specified in Section 2.1.

Code has been implemented for a discrete-time arrival generator that produces a sequence {a_n} representing the number of requests arriving in each time slot n, allowing multiple requests to arrive in the same slot.
Code has been implemented that assigns each request i an ordered tuple (v_p(i), v_d(i), z(i)) with v_p(i), v_d(i) in N and feature z(i) drawn from a finite feature set K.
The arrival implementation samples {a_n} iid and {(v_p(i), v_d(i), z(i))} iid, with the two sequences independent of each other while allowing correlation within the triple.
Empirical first-moment statistics from the arrival generator (arrival rate lambda, E[v_p], E[v_d]) match the configured parameters within reasonable Monte-Carlo tolerance over a long run.
Iteration-level batch serving with token-budget and feasibility constraints (Eqs. 2.5a-2.5d) from Section 2.1 is implemented.
Code has been implemented representing a batch as a per-request pair (delta_i^p, delta_i^d) giving the number of prefill and decode tokens from request i included in the batch.

A feasibility checker enforces Eq. (2.5a): delta_i^d > 0 is only permitted when the request's remaining unprocessed prefill count p_i' minus delta_i^p equals 0, so prefill must be finished (in this batch or earlier) before any decode token loads.
The feasibility checker enforces Eq. (2.5b): 0 <= delta_i^p <= p_i' and 0 <= delta_i^d <= d_i' for every request i in the queue.
The feasibility checker enforces Eq. (2.5c): at most one decode token per request per batch (delta_i^d in {0,1}).
The feasibility checker enforces the token budget Eq. (2.5d): sum_i (delta_i^p + delta_i^d) = b' <= b, where b is a configurable token budget.
When remaining processing time R(n) > 0, the scheduler is forced to produce b' = 0 (no new batch loaded); when R(n) = 0 an idle slot (b' = 0) is also permitted.

A behavioral unit test constructs the mini-example in Figure 2 (Requests 1-3 with the shown prefill/decode composition and token budget 6) and verifies that a Sarathi-like feasible schedule can produce token loads (6, 4, 2) across iterations 1-3.

The DTMC state representation X(n) = (R(n), {(P_i(n), D_i(n), Z_i(n)) : i in Q_n}) from Eq. (2.4) is implemented, tracking unprocessed prefill/decode counts (excluding tokens currently being processed).
Code has been implemented for a system-state object that holds the remaining-processing-time R(n) and an ordered collection Q_n of active request records with fields (P_i, D_i, Z_i).
P_i(n) and D_i(n) exclude tokens currently loaded in an in-flight batch; tokens under processing are accounted separately until the batch completes.
The ordering of Q_n (e.g., by arrival time) is preserved across time slots so that FCFS-style scheduling algorithms can access oldest-first requests.
System dynamics updating the post-decision state and the next-slot state via Eqs. (2.6a)-(2.6c), including arrivals and remaining-time countdown, are implemented.
Code has been implemented that computes the post-decision state X'(n) by subtracting the scheduled (delta_i^p, delta_i^d) from (P_i(n), D_i(n)) as per Eq. (2.6a).
New arrivals A_n in slot n are appended to Q_n' to form Q_{n+1} with their initial (P, D, Z) equal to (v_p, v_d, z) per Eq. (2.6b).
The remaining-time update sets R(n+1) = t_{b'} when a new non-empty batch of load b' is scheduled and R(n) = 0, and R(n+1) = max(R(n) - 1, 0) otherwise, matching Eq. (2.6c).
When the last decode token of a request finishes at the end of a slot (D_i drops to 0 with prefill already complete), the request is removed from Q at that slot boundary.
Batch processing spans multiple slots uninterrupted (no preemption at the token level): once R(n) is set to t_{b'}, no new batching decision is taken until R decrements to 0.
A behavioral test drives the simulator forward for a full episode and verifies conservation: total tokens departed equals sum of (v_p + v_d) over departed requests.
The scheduler interface pi(x) -> {(delta_i^p, delta_i^d)}_{i in Q(x)} is implemented as a pluggable component consumed by the DTMC engine.
Code has been implemented defining a scheduler abstract interface that takes a system state x with R(x) = 0 and returns a feasible batch configuration pi(x).

Code has been implemented for a work-conserving predicate: given state x, checks whether there exists a feasible batch with b' = b, so that any work-conserving policy must produce b' = b whenever the predicate is true.
The DTMC engine invokes pi only when R(n) = 0 and rejects any pi(x) output that violates the feasibility constraints Eqs. (2.5a)-(2.5d).
The batch processing time function t_{b'} is wired into the DTMC dynamics so that the batch of token load b' occupies exactly t_{b'} slots, with idle batches (b' = 0) taking one slot.

Code has been implemented that queries a batch-processing-time function t_{b'} (supplied by the empirical/piecewise-linear model) at each new batch decision and uses the returned integer number of slots to schedule R.
A behavioral test drives the simulator with a constant b' and confirms that batch completion events occur exactly every t_{b'} slots.
Simulator instrumentation records the standard bookkeeping quantities Z_f(n), W_f(n), B_f(n), F_f(n), E(n), V_f(N) defined in Section C.1 for downstream stability and throughput analysis.
Code has been implemented that tracks per-slot Z_p(n), Z_d(n) (number of requests in prefill and decode phase) and W_p(n), W_d(n) (number of prefill/decode tokens including those under processing).
Code has been implemented that logs cumulative counters B_p(n), B_d(n) (tokens completed in each phase), F_p(n), F_d(n) (requests completed each phase), and E(n) = sum a_l.
A behavioral test verifies the identity Z_f(n) relations (Eq. C.7-C.8): W_f(n) + B_f(n) equals V_f(E(n)) and Z_f - F_f identities hold at every slot.

A driver ties arrivals, scheduler, feasibility checker, batch-time model, and DTMC updater into an end-to-end simulator that reproduces Figure 2's iteration timeline for a supplied scheduling algorithm.
Code has been implemented for a top-level simulate(T, scheduler, arrival_process, batch_time_fn, token_budget) function that returns the full state trajectory and cumulative counters over T slots.
The simulator is deterministic given a fixed random seed, so identical (seed, config) inputs reproduce identical trajectories bit-for-bit.

The piecewise-linear batch processing time formula t_{b'} = c + a * max(b' - b_0, 0) is fitted from measurements and matches the paper's reported coefficients (e.g., c=45.5ms, a=0.30, b_0=64 for Llama-3-70B TP=2) with R^2 > 0.985.
A measurement harness for empirically profiling batch processing times over varying token loads and configurations is implemented.
Code has been implemented that drives an LLM serving backend (SGLang or equivalent) with a sweep of batch token-load values b' and records the wall-clock time of each iteration/batch.

Code has been implemented that constructs batches with a controlled total token load b' (mixing prefill and decode tokens as needed) so that b' can be swept over a range that includes values below and above b_0 up to at least 1024 tokens.

Code has been implemented that performs warmup iterations and uses CUDA synchronization (or an equivalent) before recording batch timing to ensure timings reflect steady-state GPU execution rather than kernel launch overhead.

Code has been implemented that supports profiling multiple models (at least Llama-3-1B, Llama-3-8B, CodeLlama-34B, Llama-3-70B) and multiple tensor-parallel sizes (TP=1, 2, 4) as required by Figures 3 and 4.

Code has been implemented that drives the profiling with ShareGPT-derived request prefill/decode compositions so that batch constituents vary while total token load is held fixed, matching the Figure 3 methodology.
Figure 3's claim that batch processing time is largely insensitive to batch constituents (small CoV at fixed token load, decreasing with model size) is empirically reproduced.

Code has been implemented that, for each (model, token-budget) configuration under full token load, collects many batch timings with different prefill/decode compositions and computes the coefficient of variation of batch processing time.
Code has been implemented that produces a Figure-3-style plot of batch processing time (with variation bars/whiskers) versus token budget on a log scale for the 1B, 8B, and 34B models.

The measured coefficient of variation of batch processing time at full token load decreases (or stays comparably small) as model size grows from 1B to 8B to 34B, matching the qualitative claim of Figure 3.
The piecewise-linear model t_{b'} = c + a * max(b' - b_0, 0) is fit to measured batch times and used to reproduce Figure 4.

Code has been implemented that fits the piecewise-linear function t_{b'} = c + a * max(b' - b_0, 0) to (b', measured-time) samples by jointly estimating c, a, and the knee b_0 (e.g., via grid search or nonlinear least squares).

For token loads b' <= b_0 the fitted model returns a constant value c (flat region), and for b' > b_0 it returns c + a*(b' - b_0) with a strictly positive slope a, matching the piecewise structure shown in Figure 4.
Code has been implemented that computes the coefficient of determination R^2 for the fitted piecewise-linear model against the measurement data for each (model, TP) configuration.

Code has been implemented that produces the Figure-4-style plots: scatter of measured batch processing times versus token load overlaid with the fitted piecewise-linear curves for CodeLlama-34B (TP=1,2,4) and Llama-3-70B (TP=2,4).
The fitted coefficients (c, a, b_0) match the values reported in the paper for each (model, TP) configuration within tolerance.
For Llama-3-70B on 2xA100-80GB with NVLink under TP=2, the fitted parameters satisfy c ≈ 45.5 ms, a ≈ 0.30 ms/token, and b_0 ≈ 64 tokens, matching the values highlighted in Section 2.1 and Figure 4.
For Llama-3-70B under TP=4, the fitted parameters approximately match Figure 4's reported values c ≈ 24.10 ms, a ≈ 0.148 ms/token, b_0 ≈ 64 tokens.
For CodeLlama-34B under TP=1, the fitted parameters approximately match Figure 4's reported values c ≈ 46.71 ms, a ≈ 0.289 ms/token, b_0 ≈ 128 tokens.
For CodeLlama-34B under TP=2, the fitted parameters approximately match Figure 4's reported values c ≈ 23.47 ms, a ≈ 0.145 ms/token, b_0 ≈ 96 tokens.
For CodeLlama-34B under TP=4, the fitted parameters approximately match Figure 4's reported values c ≈ 11.76 ms, a ≈ 0.068 ms/token, b_0 ≈ 64 tokens.
The fit quality R^2 exceeds 0.985 for every (model, TP) configuration reported in Figure 4.
The computed R^2 of the piecewise-linear fit is above 0.985 for CodeLlama-34B at TP=1, TP=2, and TP=4 and for Llama-3-70B at TP=2 and TP=4, matching the paper's claim.
Code has been implemented that logs and reports the fitted (c, a, b_0, R^2) tuple for every (model, TP) configuration in a tabular form so the R^2 > 0.985 claim is auditable.
The fitted t_{b'} formula is exposed as a reusable component for downstream scheduling and stability analyses.
Code has been implemented that exposes a function batch_time(b_prime, c, a, b0) returning c + a*max(b_prime - b0, 0), usable by simulation and stability-check code elsewhere in the codebase.

Code has been implemented that persists the fitted (c, a, b_0) parameters per (model, TP) configuration to a config file or serialized artifact, so that downstream experiments load the same coefficients used to validate Figure 4.

The four canonical scheduling policies (FasterTransformer decode-prioritized-no-mix, vanilla vLLM prefill-prioritized-no-mix, Orca prefill-prioritized-mixed, Sarathi-Serve decode-prioritized-chunked) plus the work-conserving (K_p, K_d)-FCFS family are implemented per Section 3.
A common scheduler interface and batch-construction primitives shared by all four policies are implemented.

Code has been implemented that defines a scheduler interface producing per-iteration batch decisions pi(x) = (delta_p_i, delta_d_i)_{i in Q}, taking the current system state (per-request unprocessed prefill counts p_i, unprocessed decode counts d_i, phase, arrival order) as input.

Code has been implemented that enforces the feasibility constraints in Eq. (2.5): (a) prefill tokens of a request must be exhausted before any decode token of that request enters a batch; (b) at most one decode token per request per batch; (c) sequential prefill-token ordering; (d) total token load b' <= token budget b.

Unit tests verify that infeasible batch proposals (mixing a decode token before all prefill tokens of that request are done, two decode tokens of the same request in one batch, or exceeding token budget b) are rejected by every scheduler implementation.
The token budget b is a configurable parameter of every scheduler and defaults / accepted values include the settings used in the paper (e.g., 128, 256, 512, 768, 1024).
Code has been implemented that permits idle iterations (b' = 0) when r = 0, and forces b' = 0 when a batch is still in progress (r > 0), matching Section 2.2 dynamics.
The FasterTransformer-style decode-prioritized, no-mixed-batching scheduler is implemented.

Code has been implemented for a scheduler that, whenever any request has p_i = 0 and d_i > 0, forms a decode-only batch by loading one decode token from each eligible request in FCFS order up to the batch-size / token-budget limit.
The FasterTransformer scheduler never mixes prefill and decode tokens in the same batch: batches are either decode-only (if any decoding request is present) or prefill-only otherwise.
Code has been implemented such that arriving prefill requests are held (not batched) while any decode request is outstanding, reproducing the blocking behavior described in Section 3 and Figure 5.

A unit test constructs the Figure 5 workload (requests A_d=2, B_d=4, C_d=3, D_d=1, E_d=1 with D,E arriving during A,B,C decoding) and asserts that the FasterTransformer scheduler produces the non-work-conserving batch sequence shown in Figure 5 (decode-only batches while D_p, E_p wait).
The vanilla vLLM prefill-prioritized, no-mixed-batching scheduler is implemented.
Code has been implemented for a scheduler that, whenever any request has p_i > 0, forms a prefill-only batch by packing prefill tokens in FCFS order up to the token/batch budget.
When no request has outstanding prefill tokens, the vanilla vLLM scheduler forms a decode-only batch containing at most one decode token per request.
The vanilla vLLM scheduler never places prefill and decode tokens in the same batch (batches are strictly prefill-only or decode-only), matching the Section 3 description.

A unit test on the Figure 5 example shows that the vanilla vLLM scheduler's second batch (a prefill-only batch of D_p, E_p while decode tokens of A/B/C are still waiting) violates work-conservation, matching Figure 5.
The Orca prefill-prioritized scheduler with mixed batching is implemented.
Code has been implemented for a scheduler that first packs prefill tokens from requests with p_i > 0 in FCFS order into the batch.

Code has been implemented that, after prefill tokens are packed, fills any remaining token-budget capacity with at most one decode token per request (from requests with p_i = 0, d_i > 0), producing mixed prefill+decode batches.

A unit test asserts that whenever the total available (prefill + decode) tokens across all requests is >= b, the Orca scheduler produces a batch with token load b' = b (satisfying the work-conserving definition in Eq. (2.6)).
A unit test on the Figure 5 workload reproduces the Orca batch trace shown in Figure 5, including the mixed batch (D_p, E_p, B_d, C_d, D_d, E_d) after prefills complete.
The Sarathi-Serve decode-prioritized chunked-prefill scheduler is implemented.
Code has been implemented that, when forming a batch, first loads at most one decode token from each request currently in the decode phase (p_i = 0, d_i > 0).

Code has been implemented that, after decode tokens are loaded, fills the remaining token-budget capacity with prefill tokens chunked from the fewest number of prefill-phase requests (in FCFS order), producing chunked-prefill mixed batches.
The Sarathi scheduler enforces the configured token budget b (e.g., 128 / 512 / 1024) as a hard cap on the sum of prefill and decode tokens per iteration.
A unit test verifies that whenever total unprocessed tokens >= b, the Sarathi-Serve scheduler produces a batch of exactly token load b (work-conserving per Eq. (2.6)).
A unit test on the Figure 5 workload reproduces the Sarathi-Serve batch trace shown in Figure 5, including chunked-prefill batches that mix decode tokens of A/B/C with partial prefill of D/E.
The (K_p, K_d)-FCFS work-conserving scheduling family from Section 2.3 is implemented as a configurable policy class.

Code has been implemented that exposes integer parameters K_p >= 1 and K_d >= 1 controlling the maximum number of oldest prefill-phase and decode-phase requests, respectively, whose tokens may be loaded in a batch.
Code has been implemented that, given K_p and K_d, restricts token loading in each phase to the K_p (resp. K_d) oldest requests (by arrival order) in that phase.

Code has been implemented so that within the K_p + K_d selected requests, the scheduler packs tokens (allowing prefill/decode mixing) up to the token budget b whenever enough unprocessed tokens are available, satisfying the work-conserving definition in Eq. (2.6).

Code has been implemented that supports pluggable inner token-selection rules (e.g., shortest-remaining-tokens-first, FCFS) applied within the K_p / K_d selected requests, per the Section 2.3 statement that the intra-K selection rule is arbitrary.
A unit test demonstrates that Orca and Sarathi-Serve schedulers can be reproduced as (K_p, K_d)-FCFS work-conserving instances with appropriate parameter and inner-rule settings.
Automated classification and diagnostic checks distinguish work-conserving from non-work-conserving policies among the implemented schedulers.
Code has been implemented that, given a scheduler and a set of test states with sum of unprocessed tokens >= b, reports whether the scheduler always achieves b' = b (work-conserving) or not.
Running the work-conserving classifier reports Orca and Sarathi-Serve as work-conserving, and FasterTransformer and vanilla vLLM as non-work-conserving, matching the Section 3 claims.

A single test harness runs all four schedulers (FasterTransformer, vanilla vLLM, Orca, Sarathi-Serve) on the Figure 5 example workload (A_d=2, B_d=4, C_d=3, D_d=1, E_d=1 with D,E arriving mid-run) and produces batch-composition traces that match the four rows of Figure 5.
Schedulers are integrated with the stochastic processing model / batch-time model so they can be driven by the simulation harness used elsewhere in the paper.

Code has been implemented that connects any of the four schedulers (plus the (K_p, K_d)-FCFS class) to the discrete-time LLM-engine simulator: at each slot with R(n)=0 the scheduler is invoked, the returned batch is processed for t_{b'} slots per Eq. (2.3), and state transitions follow Eq. (2.6a)-(2.6c).

The simulator / serving driver exposes a configuration flag (e.g., --scheduler={faster_transformer, vllm_vanilla, orca, sarathi, kp_kd_fcfs}) that selects which of the implemented policies is used for a run.

Theorem 1 (positive recurrence under work-conserving (K_p,K_d)-FCFS given load condition, and transience under overload) is stated and its proof — via both Lyapunov drift and fluid limit — is implemented/verified.

The formal statement of Theorem 1 (load condition, second-moment assumption, positive recurrence for part (a) and transience for part (b)) is encoded and its constituent conditions are computable/checkable in code.
Code has been implemented that evaluates the load condition λ(m_p + m_d) < b/t_b (Equation 2.7) given inputs (λ, m_p, m_d, b, t_b) and returns a boolean flag indicating stability regime.
Code has been implemented that evaluates the overload condition λ(m_p + m_d) > b/t_b (Equation 2.8) and identifies systems where no scheduling algorithm can stabilize the queue.

Code has been implemented that verifies the iid assumption and finite first-moment assumption on (v_p, v_d, z) and finite second-moment assumption E[D_1^2] < ∞ from empirical samples used in simulation.
The (K_p, K_d)-FCFS work-conserving scheduling algorithm family is implemented so it can be plugged into the DTMC simulator for verifying Theorem 1.
Code has been implemented that restricts token loading to at most K_p oldest prefill-phase requests and at most K_d oldest decode-phase requests according to arrival order.

Code has been implemented that enforces the work-conserving condition: whenever the total available unprocessed tokens (subject to feasibility (2.5)) meet or exceed the token budget b, the formed batch has b' = b.

Code has been implemented that verifies feasibility constraints (2.5a)-(2.5d) (prefill-before-decode ordering, ≤ unprocessed tokens, at most one decode token per request per batch, and Σ(δ_i^p + δ_i^d) ≤ b) for every batch produced.
Unit test: given a queue whose feasible unprocessed tokens sum to ≥ b, the work-conserving (K_p,K_d)-FCFS scheduler returns a batch with token load exactly b (or exactly the feasible max when <b).
The Lyapunov-drift proof of Theorem 1(a) is implemented and numerically verified on the DTMC for bounded token-size random variables.

Code has been implemented that computes the Lyapunov function f(X) = Σ_{i∈Q(X)} [ (1(p_i'>0) + d_i') * (something proportional to remaining workload) ] as defined in Appendix B (Equation preceding B.1).

Code has been implemented that computes the one-step conditional drift E[f(X(n+1)) - f(X(n)) | X(n) = x] under a work-conserving (K_p,K_d)-FCFS policy via Monte Carlo averaging over arrivals and token-size samples.
Code has been implemented that identifies the finite exceptional set C = {X : f(X) < B} for B := 2b(4Lb/(ελ))^2 + b and confirms Foster-Lyapunov negative drift outside C.

Measured: empirical one-step drift E[Δf(X)] evaluated at states with f(X) ≥ B under a work-conserving (K_p,K_d)-FCFS policy is strictly negative (≤ -b), consistent with the bound derived in Appendix B.

The fluid model equations (C.10)-(C.17) and stability definitions (Definitions 1-4, Proposition 2) are implemented and used to numerically verify fluid-model stability under load condition and weak instability under overload.
Code has been implemented that instantiates the fluid model state (B(t), F(t), W(t), Z(t)) and enforces fluid model equations (C.10)-(C.14) as constraints in a numerical fluid solver.
Code has been implemented that enforces the work-conserving fluid model equation (C.17): whenever W_p(t) + W_d(t) > 0 at a regular time t, dot{B}_p(t) + dot{B}_d(t) = b/t_b.
Code has been implemented that computes the total-workload Lyapunov function f(t) = m_p * Z_p(t) + (m_p + m_d) * Z_d(t) (Equation C.19) and its derivative along fluid solutions.

Code has been implemented that, at every regular point of a fluid solution with f(t) > 0 under load condition (C.1), verifies dot{f}(t) = λ(m_p + m_d) - b/t_p and confirms this value is strictly negative.
Measured: for any fluid model solution with |Z(0)| ≤ 1 under load condition (C.1), the numerical solver reaches Z(t) = 0 by time t ≥ f(0)/δ where δ = b/t_p - λ(m_p + m_d), matching Proposition 2(a).
Measured: for a fluid solution starting from 0 under overload condition (C.18), the numerical solver yields Z_p(a) + Z_d(a) ≠ 0 for some a > 0, confirming weak instability (Proposition 2(b)).
Fluid limits are constructed from fluid-scaled DTMC sample paths and shown numerically to converge to fluid model solutions, justifying use of the fluid technique in the proof of Theorem 1.
Code has been implemented that applies the fluid scaling B^{|x|}_f(t) = B_f(|x|t)/|x|, F^{|x|}_f, W^{|x|}_f, Z^{|x|}_f (Section C.3) to sample-path trajectories from the DTMC simulator.
Code has been implemented that verifies the SLLN limits (C.22): (1/N) Σ v_p(i) → m_p and (1/N) Σ v_d(i) → m_d, and empirical arrival-count average → λ, for large N drawn from the simulator.

Measured: as |x| → ∞ along a chosen sequence, the fluid-scaled trajectories (B^{|x|}, F^{|x|}, W^{|x|}, Z^{|x|}) converge uniformly on compact intervals to a Lipschitz-continuous fluid model solution satisfying (C.10)-(C.17) within numerical tolerance.
The end-to-end DTMC-level claims of Theorem 1 (positive recurrence of {X_n} under (a), transience |X(n)|/n → positive constant under (b)) are verified via long-horizon Monte Carlo simulation.

Code has been implemented that simulates the DTMC {X_n} under a work-conserving (K_p,K_d)-FCFS scheduling algorithm with configurable (λ, m_p, m_d, b, t_b) and records the total token count |X(n)| = Σ (P_i(n) + D_i(n)) over time.

Measured: under load condition (2.7), the empirical return time to the state 0 in the simulated DTMC has finite mean across independent runs, providing numerical evidence of positive recurrence (Theorem 1(a)).
Measured: under overload condition (2.8), the simulated ratio |X(n)|/n converges to λ(m_p + m_d) - b/t_b > 0 in probability as n grows, matching Theorem 1(b).
Measured: under load condition (2.7), the time-averaged |X(n)|/n from the DTMC simulator tends to 0 as n → ∞, consistent with positive recurrence and finite stationary expectation.

The instability of FasterTransformer and vanilla vLLM versus stability of Sarathi-Serve (token budget 512) is reproduced using CodeLlama-34B on A100 with homogeneous requests (avg 129 prefill, 112 decode tokens, 14.3 QPS) producing queue-length trajectories matching Figure 1.
The workload generator producing homogeneous requests matching the Figure 1 setup is implemented.
Code has been implemented that generates homogeneous requests with an average of 129 prefill tokens and 112 decode tokens per request (matching Figure 1 caption).
Code has been implemented that submits requests to the LLM serving system at a Poisson (or comparable stochastic) arrival rate of 14.3 queries per second.
The workload driver runs for at least 800 seconds of simulated wall-clock time to reproduce the time axis of Figure 1.
Empirical mean prefill token count of generated requests is within a small tolerance of 129 tokens.
Empirical mean decode token count of generated requests is within a small tolerance of 112 tokens.
Empirical arrival rate measured over the run is within a small tolerance of 14.3 QPS.
The three scheduler configurations under comparison in Figure 1 are set up and executable end-to-end.
Code has been implemented to serve CodeLlama-34B under a FasterTransformer-style decode-prioritized non-mixed-batching scheduler.
Code has been implemented to serve CodeLlama-34B under a vanilla vLLM prefill-prioritized non-mixed-batching scheduler (chunked prefill disabled).
Code has been implemented to serve CodeLlama-34B under Sarathi-Serve with token budget configured to 512.
All three schedulers are executed on a single A100 GPU (or documented equivalent) with the same CodeLlama-34B checkpoint and identical workload seed for a fair comparison.

Memory/KV-cache limits are configured large enough (or bypassed as in the paper's non-memory-constrained assumption) so that request blocking due to memory does not confound the stability observation.
Queue-length trajectory instrumentation and plotting reproduce the format of Figure 1.
Code has been implemented that logs the number of requests currently in the system as a function of time for each scheduler run.
Code has been implemented that renders a plot with time (seconds, 0-800+) on the x-axis and requests-in-system on the y-axis with one curve per scheduler, matching Figure 1's layout.
The measured queue-length trajectories reproduce the qualitative and quantitative instability/stability claims of Figure 1.
Under the FasterTransformer scheduler, the requests-in-system trajectory grows unboundedly over the 800s window (monotonically increasing trend), demonstrating instability.
Under vanilla vLLM (no chunked prefill), the requests-in-system trajectory also grows unboundedly over the 800s window, demonstrating instability.
Under Sarathi-Serve with token budget 512, the requests-in-system trajectory remains bounded (does not grow without bound) over the 800s window, demonstrating stability.
The FasterTransformer requests-in-system count at t=800s reaches on the order of several thousand requests, consistent with the ~6000-8000 range shown in Figure 1.
The vanilla vLLM requests-in-system count at t=800s reaches on the order of several thousand requests, consistent with Figure 1's terminal value for vLLM.
The Sarathi-Serve (token budget 512) requests-in-system count stays within a small bounded range (well under 500) throughout the 800s window, consistent with the flat curve near zero in Figure 1.

The offered load computed as lambda*(m_p + m_d)*t_b/b for the Figure 1 workload satisfies the stability condition (2.7) (i.e., is strictly less than 1) for CodeLlama-34B with the fitted (c, a, b_0) parameters, confirming that instability of FT/vLLM is not due to overload.
Proposition 1 (stability of K parallel identical LLM engines under work-conserving (K_p,K_d)-FCFS with random or join-lowest load balancing under load condition (4.1)) is reproduced.
The K homogeneous parallel LLM engine system is implemented, including K identical single-engine simulators plus a load balancer front-end.

Code has been implemented that instantiates K identical LLM engine simulators, each running the discrete-time stochastic processing model from Section 2 with the same batch-processing-time parameters (c, a, b_0) and token budget b.

Code has been implemented that maintains, for each engine k in {1,...,K}, its own state X^k(n) = (R^k(n), {(P_i^k, D_i^k, Z_i^k)}) and independently applies a work-conserving (K_p, K_d)-FCFS scheduling algorithm inside that engine.

Code has been implemented that draws request arrivals to the K-engine system as an i.i.d. sequence with total arrival rate lambda and token sizes (v_p(i), v_d(i)) drawn i.i.d., consistent with assumption (2.1)-(2.2).
The load-balancing policies used to route arriving requests to one of the K engines are implemented.
Code has been implemented for the random (uniform) load balancer that assigns each arriving request to engine k in {1,...,K} independently with probability 1/K.

Code has been implemented for the join-lowest-load load balancer that routes an arriving request to argmin_k f^k(t), where f^k(t) is the total unprocessed token workload at engine k (i.e., m_p * Z_p^k + (m_p + m_d) * Z_d^k or an equivalent workload proxy).
The join-lowest-load balancer breaks ties among engines with equal minimum workload deterministically or uniformly at random, and the tie-breaking rule is documented and consistent across runs.
The load condition (4.1) lambda * (m_p + m_d) < K * b / t_b is enforced/verified in the experimental configuration.

Code has been implemented that computes the per-engine load rho = lambda * (m_p + m_d) / (K * b / t_b) from the configured arrival rate, mean token sizes, token budget, batch processing time, and K, and asserts rho < 1 before running the parallel-engine simulation.
A stability diagnostic that tracks per-engine and system-wide occupancy over time is implemented for the K-engine system.
Code has been implemented that records, at each time step n, the number of outstanding requests |Q_n^k| and total outstanding tokens |X^k(n)| for every engine k, and the aggregate across engines.
Code has been implemented that estimates stability by checking that the time-averaged queue length over the second half of the run is bounded and does not exhibit a positive linear trend versus time.
Empirical verification that the K-engine system is positive recurrent (stable) under Proposition 1's assumptions is demonstrated.

Under a work-conserving (K_p, K_d)-FCFS scheduler at every engine combined with the random load balancer, and with lambda * (m_p + m_d) < K * b / t_b, the measured aggregate token count remains bounded (does not diverge) over a long simulation horizon.

Under a work-conserving (K_p, K_d)-FCFS scheduler at every engine combined with the join-lowest-load balancer, and with lambda * (m_p + m_d) < K * b / t_b, the measured aggregate token count remains bounded over a long simulation horizon.

When the load is scaled just above the threshold (lambda * (m_p + m_d) > K * b / t_b), the K-engine simulator produces a queue length trajectory that grows approximately linearly in time, consistent with Theorem 1(b) / weak instability.
Fluid-model stability arguments for a single engine serving two request types (Section 4.2) and the four-agent fork-join network conjecture (Section 4.3) are reproduced.
The two-type single-engine setup (Section 4.2) with type-specific arrival rates and mean token sizes is modeled, and the fluid-based stability argument under Eq. (4.2) is reproduced.

Code has been implemented that defines a single LLM engine model serving two request types j in {1,2}, each with its own arrival rate lambda^j and mean prefill/decode token sizes (m_p^j, m_d^j), producing arrivals from independent per-type processes into a shared queue.

Code has been implemented that evaluates the two-type load condition sum_{j in {1,2}} lambda^j (m_p^j + m_d^j) < b/t_b (Equation 4.2) from user-supplied parameters and returns whether the condition holds.
Code has been implemented that computes the total-workload Lyapunov function f(t) = sum_j m_p^j Z_p^j(t) + (m_p^j + m_d^j) Z_d^j(t) (Equation 4.3) from the fluid state of both request types.

Code has been implemented that runs a work-conserving (K_p, K_d)-FCFS scheduling algorithm on the two-type single-engine fluid/discrete simulator, ensuring that whenever total unprocessed tokens are positive, the batch is filled to token budget b as in Eq. (2.6).

Code has been implemented that, at regular points where f(t) > 0, verifies numerically that the derivative satisfies d/dt(B_p + B_d) = b/t_b under the work-conserving policy in the two-type fluid model.

Code has been implemented that computes the negative drift constant delta = b/t_b - sum_j lambda^j (m_p^j + m_d^j) and demonstrates that the Lyapunov function f(t) reaches zero by time f(0)/delta in the two-type fluid trajectory, confirming stability under condition (4.2).

In a two-type simulation with parameters satisfying Eq. (4.2), the measured total workload f(t) empirically hits zero within a small multiple (e.g., <= 2x) of the theoretical bound f(0)/delta, matching the fluid-model stability prediction of Section 4.2.
The four-agent fork-join LLM network of Section 4.3 is implemented and Conjecture 1's per-agent load condition is verified as the throughput-optimality criterion.

Code has been implemented that constructs a network of four LLM agents indexed j in {0,1,2,3}, where requests arrive at agent 0 at rate lambda, fork into two sub-tasks after agent 0 that are routed to agents 1 and 2 respectively, and are joined before entering agent 3.

Code has been implemented that models per-agent token sizes (m_p^j, m_d^j) for each j in {0,1,2,3} and passes token counts along the fork-join workflow so downstream agents receive the appropriate token load per sub-request.

Code has been implemented that implements the fork-join synchronization: agent 3 only starts processing the merged request after both sub-tasks from agents 1 and 2 belonging to the same original request have completed.
Code has been implemented that runs a work-conserving (K_p^j, K_d^j)-FCFS scheduling algorithm independently at each of the four agents in the fork-join network.
Code has been implemented that checks Conjecture 1's load condition lambda (m_p^j + m_d^j) < b/t_b for every agent j in {0,1,2,3} and reports per-agent slack.

Code has been implemented that reduces the four-agent fork-join network to the two-agent subsystem (dropping agent 3) and verifies via fluid-limit simulation that positive recurrence holds under Conjecture 1's per-agent load condition for j in {0,1,2}.

In a fork-join simulation with all four per-agent load conditions of Conjecture 1 satisfied, the total number of requests across the network remains bounded (does not diverge) over a long horizon, providing empirical support for the conjectured stability.

In a fork-join simulation where at least one agent violates its Conjecture 1 load condition (lambda (m_p^j + m_d^j) >= b/t_b), the number of tokens at that agent grows without bound while other agents may remain stable, matching the necessity of the per-agent condition.

The two-agent Rybko-Stolyar (RS) type LLM network simulation from Section 4.3 is reproduced: under ρ=0.9, b=768, t_b=1, and Poisson token sizes per equations (4.4)-(4.5), the specified work-conserving priority policy (Figure 8 Up) exhibits unbounded queue growth while the reversed priority policy (Figure 8 Down) achieves stability.
The RS-type two-agent network topology and request-flow structure are implemented per Figure 7.

Code has been implemented that instantiates exactly two LLM engine agents (agent 1 and agent 2), each modeled as an independent LLM inference engine following the stochastic processing model of Section 2.

Code has been implemented that defines two request types A and B, where type A requires processing first at agent 1 (short prefill, short decode) then at agent 2 (long prefill, short decode), and type B requires processing first at agent 2 (short prefill, short decode) then at agent 1 (long prefill, short decode).

Code has been implemented that routes each request between agents 1 and 2 in the correct order based on its type (A or B), and marks the request as departed only after both sub-tasks are completed in sequence.
Code has been implemented that maintains, at each agent, separate state for outstanding type-A sub-tasks and type-B sub-tasks (with their prefill and decode token counts).
The workload parameters (arrival process, token size distributions, load, and batch parameters) match the RS experiment specification.
Code has been implemented that generates request arrivals as a Poisson process with equal arrival rates for type A and type B such that the total system load equals ρ = 0.9.

Code has been implemented that samples per-sub-task prefill and decode token counts as independent Poisson random variables with the means specified by equations (4.4) and (4.5) of the paper (short means for short tasks, long means for long tasks at each agent).
Each agent uses a token budget b = 768 tokens per batch as specified in Section 4.3.
Each batch (whether full or partial) requires exactly one discrete time slot to process, i.e., t_b = 1, and this holds regardless of the token load b'.
The configured arrival rate and mean token sizes produce a total per-agent load of ρ = 0.9 (i.e., λ·(m_p + m_d)·t_b/b = 0.9 at each agent) as verified by a numerical check in the simulation setup.
Both the unstable work-conserving priority policy and its reversed-priority stable counterpart are implemented at each agent.
Code has been implemented so that under the unstable policy (Figure 8 Up), agent 1 gives non-preemptive priority to type B sub-tasks over type A sub-tasks.
Code has been implemented so that under the unstable policy (Figure 8 Up), agent 2 gives non-preemptive priority to type A sub-tasks over type B sub-tasks.
Within each request type, the scheduler at each agent uses decode-priority FCFS (decode tokens are loaded before prefill tokens, and among tokens of the same phase FCFS order is used).

At agent 1, type A and type B tokens are mixed in a single batch only when the higher-priority type (B) cannot by itself form a full batch of size b; agent 2 follows the symmetric rule (mixing only when priority type A cannot fill the batch).

Code has been implemented such that both policies are work-conserving: whenever tokens are available across the two types and the token budget b = 768 can be filled (possibly by mixing), a full batch of b tokens is loaded.

Code has been implemented for the reversed-priority (stable) variant (Figure 8 Down): agent 1 gives non-preemptive priority to type A sub-tasks and agent 2 gives non-preemptive priority to type B sub-tasks, with the same within-type decode-priority FCFS and mixing rule as the unstable policy.
The discrete-time simulation runs long enough and logs the necessary quantities to reproduce Figure 8.

Code has been implemented that advances the system in discrete time slots, processing at most one batch per agent per slot in accordance with t_b = 1, and applying arrivals, batch formation, batch completion, and routing per slot.
Code has been implemented that logs the total number of outstanding requests at agent 1 and at agent 2 over simulation time (for both policies).
Code has been implemented that logs the total number of unprocessed tokens (prefill + decode) at agent 1 and at agent 2 over simulation time (for both policies).
The simulation horizon extends to at least 10^5 time slots so that Figure 8 [Up] can show growth over ~10^2 to 10^5 slots and Figure 8 [Down] can be shown over the interval [96500, 100000].

Code has been implemented that produces four log-scale plots analogous to Figure 8: for each policy (unstable Up, stable Down), one plot of #requests vs time and one plot of #tokens vs time, each showing curves for agent 1 and agent 2 separately.
The measured simulation outputs match the qualitative and quantitative claims about instability under the specified priority and stability under its reversal.

Under the unstable policy (Figure 8 Up), the total number of tokens across both agents grows without bound over time, reaching on the order of 10^6-10^7 tokens by time ~10^5, consistent with Figure 8 [Up] right panel.
Under the unstable policy (Figure 8 Up), the total number of outstanding requests at both agents grows over time to on the order of 10^4-10^5 by time ~10^5, consistent with Figure 8 [Up] left panel.

Under the reversed (stable) policy (Figure 8 Down), the total number of tokens at each agent remains bounded over the observation window [96500, 100000], staying on the order of at most ~10^4 as in Figure 8 [Down] right panel.

Under the reversed (stable) policy (Figure 8 Down), the total number of outstanding requests at each agent remains bounded (on the order of at most ~10^2) over the window [96500, 100000], consistent with Figure 8 [Down] left panel.

The experiment confirms that instability occurs under the specified work-conserving priority policy even though ρ = 0.9 < 1, demonstrating that not all work-conserving policies stabilize the RS-type network.

Experimental configuration matches the paper's Figure 9 setup: CodeLlama-34B on Sarathi-Serve with scaled production conversation traces and three token-budget sweeps.

Code has been implemented to load the CodeLlama-34B model in Sarathi-Serve with the same tensor-parallel and GPU configuration used to generate the piecewise-linear batch time coefficients (c=46.71, a=0.289, b0=128) reported for CodeLlama-34B in Figure 4.
Code has been implemented to launch Sarathi-Serve as the LLM serving engine with chunked-prefill enabled and configurable token budget passed via a CLI/config parameter.
Code has been implemented to sweep exactly the three token-budget values {128, 512, 1024} and run one full experiment for each while holding all other parameters fixed.
Code has been implemented to load a production conversation trace (real prompt/response length distribution) and drive requests into the serving engine according to the trace's arrival timestamps.

Instrumentation that records per-request TTFT and end-to-end latency and produces CCDF curves matching Figure 9's axes.

Code has been implemented to record end-to-end latency (arrival to final decode token departure) for every request.
Code has been implemented to compute the complementary CDF (CCDF) of the recorded latency samples for both E2E and prefill (TTFT) metrics per token-budget setting.
Code has been implemented to extract the median (50th percentile) of the E2E and TTFT distributions for each of the three token budgets and report them in the same ms units as Figure 9.

Measured median end-to-end latency values match the paper's reported figures for each token budget.
The median end-to-end latency for Sarathi-Serve with token budget 128 on CodeLlama-34B matches the paper-reported value of 75.97 ms.
The median end-to-end latency for Sarathi-Serve with token budget 512 on CodeLlama-34B matches the paper-reported value of 94.23 ms.

The median TTFT for Sarathi-Serve with token budget 512 on CodeLlama-34B matches the paper-reported value of 113.37 ms.
The median TTFT for Sarathi-Serve with token budget 1024 on CodeLlama-34B matches the paper-reported value of 178.65 ms.
Qualitative trade-off observations reported alongside Figure 9 hold in the reproduced data.
The reproduced results show that the moderate token budget (512) yields the lowest median E2E latency among the three settings, matching the qualitative claim in Section 5.

The reproduced results show that increasing the token budget beyond 128 does not increase, and for budget 512 slightly reduces, median TTFT compared to budget 128, reflecting the paper's claim that overly small budgets (128) incur significant TTFT overhead from repeated cross-attention.
The extended batch-processing-time model incorporating attention computation (Appendix A.1) and the piecewise KV-cache overhead model (Appendix A.2) are implemented as described.
The extended batch processing time model with attention computation (Appendix A.1) is implemented.

Code has been implemented that defines a batch processing time function for batch n as t_{b'} = c + a * max(b' - b_0, 0) + alpha * sum_{i in batch}(delta_i^p * (bar_P_i(n) + bar_D_i(n))) + beta * sum_{i in batch}(delta_i^d * (bar_P_i(n) + bar_D_i(n))), matching the formula in Appendix A.1.

Code has been implemented that maintains, per request i and per batch n, the cumulative counts bar_P_i(n) of processed prompt tokens and bar_D_i(n) of decoded tokens up to and including batch n, and exposes these state variables to the batch-time model.

Code has been implemented that treats the attention-cost coefficients alpha and beta as configurable model/hardware-dependent constants, loadable from a configuration for at least the CodeLlama-34B and Llama-3-70B configurations used in the paper.

When alpha = beta = 0, the extended batch-processing-time function reduces exactly to the short-context piecewise-linear form t_{b'} = c + a * max(b' - b_0, 0), verified by a unit test comparing outputs on a set of representative token loads b'.

A unit test verifies that with nonzero alpha and beta, the batch-processing-time output increases monotonically as the cumulative context lengths bar_P_i + bar_D_i of tokens included in the batch grow (holding token load b' fixed), reflecting the non-linear long-context behavior described in Appendix A.1.
The piecewise KV-cache memory-overhead model (Appendix A.2) is implemented.
Code has been implemented that computes, per request i, the number x_i of KV tokens exceeding the configured memory limit, given the request's current KV footprint and the engine's KV-cache capacity.

Code has been implemented that defines the piecewise overhead function o(x_i) with two regimes (e.g., swap/offload regime a_1 * x_i + b_1 and recomputation regime a_2 * x_i + b_2) as specified in Appendix A.2, and selects between them according to the configured KV policy.

The coefficients (a_1, a_2, b_1, b_2) of the piecewise overhead model are exposed as configuration parameters tied to system-level quantities (CPU-GPU bandwidth, chunk size, hidden dimension, and other model configuration), rather than hard-coded.
A unit test verifies that o(x_i) = 0 when x_i <= 0 (i.e., the request fits in KV cache), and that o(x_i) is non-negative and piecewise-linear in x_i for x_i > 0 under each of the two policy branches.

Code has been implemented that composes the KV-overhead o(x_i) additively into the extended batch processing time function from Appendix A.1, so the total per-batch time reflects both attention cost and KV-memory overhead when both are enabled.
The fluid model equations (C.10)-(C.17), definitions of stability/weak instability, Proposition 2, and the fluid-limit construction (Lemma 1-3) proving each limit is a fluid solution are reproduced.
The bookkeeping quantities and dynamic equations of the LLM engine (Appendix C.1) that underlie the fluid model are implemented.

Code has been implemented that maintains the per-slot quantities Z_p(n), Z_d(n), W_p(n), W_d(n), B_p(n), B_d(n), F_p(n), F_d(n), E(n), and V_p(N), V_d(N) as defined in Appendix C.1 for a single LLM engine, updating them each iteration from arrivals, batching decisions, and completions.

Code has been implemented that enforces the flow-conservation identities of Appendix C.1 (linking Z_f, W_f, B_f, F_f, V_f, and E) so that at every simulated time slot the accounting equations hold exactly under any (K_p, K_d)-FCFS scheduling algorithm.

Code has been implemented that realizes the (K_p, K_d)-FCFS key relationship (Eq. C.9 in Appendix C.1) governing which oldest requests contribute prefill/decode tokens to a batch, matching the same structural form as Eq. (6.51) of Dai & Harrison (2020).
The fluid model equations (C.10)-(C.17), together with the notion of regular points and work-conserving fluid solutions, are encoded as verifiable properties.

Code has been implemented that represents fluid-model equations (C.10)-(C.11) relating Z_f(t), F_f(t), and arrival counts for phases f in {p, d}, and that can numerically check them for any candidate fluid trajectory.

Code has been implemented that enforces fluid-model equation (C.12): B_f(·) is Lipschitz with constant b/t_b, i.e. B_f(t)-B_f(s) ≤ (b/t_b)(t-s) for all 0≤s≤t and f∈{p,d}, and provides a checker function that verifies this on discrete samples of a fluid solution.
Code has been implemented that encodes fluid-model equations (C.13) and (C.14) linking F_f(·), B_f(·), and W_f(·), and verifies Lipschitz continuity of the resulting F_f and W_f components.

Code has been implemented that encodes the work-conserving fluid-model equation (C.17): at any regular point t with W_p(t)+W_d(t) > 0, the derivative sum \dot B_p(t)+\dot B_d(t) equals b/t_b, and provides a numerical test that this holds for fluid solutions produced under work-conserving (K_p,K_d)-FCFS algorithms.

Code has been implemented that identifies regular points of a fluid solution (points where the vector-valued state function is differentiable) as defined in Definition 1, and exposes an API for querying derivatives at such points.
The stability and weak-instability definitions (Definitions 3 and 4) and the workload Lyapunov function of Proposition 2 are implemented.

Code has been implemented that checks fluid-model stability per Definition 3: given any fluid solution with |Z(0)| = Z_p(0)+Z_d(0) ≤ 1, it verifies existence of a fixed δ > 0 such that Z(t)=0 for t≥δ.
Code has been implemented that checks fluid-model weak instability per Definition 4: given any fluid solution starting from 0, it verifies existence of a fixed a > 0 with Z_p(a)+Z_d(a) ≠ 0.

Code has been implemented that computes the workload Lyapunov function f(t) = m_p Z_p(t) + (m_p+m_d) Z_d(t) (Eq. C.19) used in the proof of Proposition 2, along with its almost-everywhere derivative on a fluid solution.
Proposition 2 (fluid-model stability under load condition (C.1) and weak instability under overload (C.18)) is verified numerically on generated fluid solutions.

Code has been implemented that, given λ, m_p, m_d, b, t_p, and a work-conserving (K_p,K_d)-FCFS fluid solution satisfying load condition (C.1), computes \dot f(t) at regular points where f(t)>0 and verifies it equals λ(m_p+m_d) - b/t_p, which is strictly negative.

For a work-conserving fluid solution with |Z(0)|≤1 under load condition (C.1), the implementation numerically verifies Proposition 2(a) by showing f(t) reaches 0 no later than f(0)/δ with δ = b/t_p - λ(m_p+m_d), and Z(t)=0 thereafter.

Code has been implemented that, under overload condition (C.18) λ(m_p+m_d) > b/t_p, generates a fluid solution starting from 0 under an arbitrary scheduling algorithm and verifies that f(t) = (λ(m_p+m_d) - b/t_p)·t at regular points, so f(a)>0 (hence Z_p(a)+Z_d(a)≠0) for any a>0, matching Proposition 2(b).
The fluid-limit construction of Appendix C.3, including scaled processes and Lemmas 1-3 showing each limit is a fluid solution, is implemented and validated.

Code has been implemented that constructs the fluid-scaled processes \bar B_f^x, \bar E^x, \bar F_f^x, \bar W_f^x, \bar Z_f^x from a stochastic simulation of the LLM engine starting at state x with |x|>0, using the scaling in Eq. (C.22).

Code has been implemented that verifies the SLLN-type limits of Eq. (C.22)-(C.23) on scaled arrival and token-size processes, checking convergence of \bar E^x(t) to λ t and of V_p, V_d scaling to m_p t and m_d t along sequences with |x_k|→∞.

Code has been implemented that reproduces Lemma 1: given a sample path in the full-measure set Ω_0 and an unbounded set A⊆X, it extracts a subsequence {x_k}⊆A with |x_k|→∞ for which the fluid-scaled process (\bar B_p^{x_k}(·),\bar B_d^{x_k}(·)) converges uniformly on compact sets to a Lipschitz limit (\hat B_p(·),\hat B_d(·)).

Code has been implemented that reproduces Lemma 2: from the limit (\hat B_p,\hat B_d) of Lemma 1 and the SLLN limits of Eq. (C.22), it constructs the corresponding limiting functions (\hat F_p,\hat F_d,\hat W_p,\hat W_d,\hat Z_p,\hat Z_d) and verifies uniform-on-compacts convergence along the same subsequence.

Code has been implemented that reproduces Lemma 3: it verifies that every fluid limit (\hat B,\hat F,\hat W,\hat Z) satisfies all fluid-model equations (C.10)-(C.14), and additionally (C.17) when the underlying scheduling algorithm is work-conserving, thereby confirming it is a (work-conserving) fluid solution.

Using the fluid-limit code, an experiment is run where the LLM engine DTMC is simulated under a work-conserving (K_p,K_d)-FCFS algorithm from large initial states x with |x|→∞ (load condition (C.1) satisfied), and the fluid-scaled \bar Z^x(t) is shown to hit 0 by t≤ f(0)/δ as predicted by Proposition 2(a), confirming numerically that the empirical limit matches a stable fluid solution.
